publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: A dynamic network model of temporal receptive fields in primary auditory cortex

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: why cortical auditory responses appear to depend on hundreds of milliseconds of sound history when the delays available to the circuit are far shorter
span.quote: Auditory neurons encode stimulus history, which is often modelled using a span of time-delays in a spectro-temporal receptive field (STRF). We propose an alternative model for the encoding of stimulus history, which we apply to extracellular recordings of neurons in the primary auditory cortex of anaesthetized ferrets. For a linear-non-linear STRF model (LN model) to achieve a high level of performance in predicting single unit neural responses to natural sounds in the primary auditory cortex, we found that it is necessary to include time delays going back at least 200 ms in the past. This is an unrealistic time span for biological delay lines.

span.label: how much of the long temporal receptive field can be produced by neurons' own decaying memory rather than by long delay lines
span.quote: We constructed a neural-network model whose output is the weighted sum of units whose responses are determined by a dynamic firing-rate equation. The dynamic aspect performs low-pass filtering on each unit’s response, providing an exponentially decaying memory whose time constant is individual to each unit.

span.label: shows a network whose units each carry their own exponential decay matches a 200 ms delay-line model using only 25 ms of delay, which is within the biologically available range
span.quote: We find that this dynamic network (DNet) model, when fitted to the neural data using STRFs of only 25 ms duration, can achieve prediction performance on a held-out dataset comparable to the best performing LN model with STRFs of 200 ms duration.

span.label: method
span.quote: We propose an alternative model for the encoding of stimulus history, which we apply to extracellular recordings of neurons in the primary auditory cortex of anaesthetized ferrets.

span.label: temporal receptive fields in primary auditory cortex
span.quote: Auditory neurons encode stimulus history, which is often modelled using a span of time-delays in a spectro-temporal receptive field (STRF).

span.label: simulation
span.quote: We constructed a neural-network model whose output is the weighted sum of units whose responses are determined by a dynamic firing-rate equation.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: membrane capacitance and resistance make firing rate a low-pass-filtered version of synaptic current, so each unit's output is convolved with an exponentially decaying impulse response that stores recent input
span.quote: Due to the capacitance and resistance of the neural cell membrane, the membrane potential and hence the firing rate is approximately a low-pass filtered version of the synaptic current.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: integration by membrane time constants (or other exponentially decaying memory processes) rather than long delay lines produces the apparent long temporal receptive fields of cortical neurons
span.quote: These findings suggest that integration due to the membrane time constants or other exponentially-decaying memory processes may underlie linear temporal receptive fields of neurons beyond 25 ms.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: the long narrowband inhibitory fields seen in fitted STRFs are the signature of short inhibitory inputs passed through slowly decaying memory, not of genuinely delayed inhibition
span.quote: This suggests that these temporally extended inhibitory fields in STRFs may reflect neural mechanisms that can be approximated by exponentially-decaying memory processes.

span.label: membrane capacitance and resistance make firing rate a low-pass filtered version of synaptic current, which is the decay the model implements
span.quote: Due to the capacitance and resistance of the neural cell membrane, the membrane potential and hence the firing rate is approximately a low-pass filtered version of the synaptic current. A common simple dynamic model of neurons that captures this phenomenon is the differential equation ( Eq 7 ) known as the firing-rate equation

span.label: both parts are needed: a single dynamic unit does worse than a plain LN model, so the effect requires decay AND a network
span.quote: A single-unit dynamic model was also developed to examine the effect of a time constant in an LN-like single STRF model. Prediction performance of this model was found to be worse than the LN model ( Fig 6B ). This indicates that both long time constants and a network architecture are needed for the 25-ms DNet model to achieve prediction performance similar to that of standard models.

span.label: all the dynamic processes listed could be captured by the same exponentially-decaying memory, and the paper says they are not exclusive of one another
span.quote: We note, however, that although the DNet model was developed with membrane dynamics in mind, aspects of all the above listed dynamic processes could be captured by the same exponentially-decaying memory in the DNet. These different processes are not exclusive of each other, and combinations of them may contribute to the effects we find.

span.label: a time constant before the nonlinearity explains much of the variance, and moving it after the nonlinearity improves prediction further
span.quote: The sDNet model achieves best performance in predicting neural responses when the duration of the STRFs is 200 ms (CC norm = 0.71) ( Fig 8A ). Although the sDNet with 25-ms STRFs predicts neural responses better (CC norm = 0.67) than the 25-ms LN model (CC norm = 0.51) and the 25-ms NRF model (CC norm = 0.51), it is worse than the 25-ms DNet model (CC norm = 0.71). This suggests that a large percentage of the variance of neural responses can be explained by a time constant before non-linearity, but that having a time constant after the non-linearity further improves prediction.

span.label: the units that carry the long time constants are almost all inhibitory, which was not built in
span.quote: We found that almost all units having large time constants are inhibitory in nature

span.label: The DNet sometimes fails to reach fits it should in principle attain, suggesting optimisation failure or overfitting
span.quote: The fact that this is not the case suggests that, at least in some cases, the very best fits are not being found for the DNet model, perhaps as a consequence of some overfitting.

span.label: Long-latency thalamic inputs cannot be ruled out as a partial explanation
span.quote: Hence, we cannot rule out the possibility that long-latency inputs at least partially explain the dependence of auditory cortical neurons on stimulus history–indeed it is likely that they do to some extent.

span.label: History dependence out to seconds is captured by neither standard models nor the DNet
span.quote: This indicates that there are some nonlinear dynamic processes that provide history dependence which cannot be captured either by a linear or LN models, nor by the DNet model.

span.label: The model can only express exponential temporal dynamics
span.quote: Perhaps this is because the DNet model has limited capacity to capture temporal dynamics that are not exponential in nature.

span.label: long-latency thalamic inputs cannot be ruled out and probably do contribute to some degree
span.quote: Hence, we cannot rule out the possibility that long-latency inputs at least partially explain the dependence of auditory cortical neurons on stimulus history–indeed it is likely that they do to some extent.

span.label: A1 responses depend on history out to about 4 seconds, which neither linear models nor this one can capture
span.quote: The firing rate of A1 neurons has been demonstrated to depend on stimulus history up to ~4 s in the past [ 17 ]. This dependence cannot be fully captured by linear models such as STRFs (17). This indicates that there are some nonlinear dynamic processes that provide history dependence which cannot be captured either by a linear or LN models, nor by the DNet model. Perhaps this is because the DNet model has limited capacity to capture temporal dynamics that are not exponential in nature.

span.label: where the DNet underperforms, the paper reads it as the best fits not being found rather than as a property of the model class
span.quote: The fact that this is not the case suggests that, at least in some cases, the very best fits are not being found for the DNet model, perhaps as a consequence of some overfitting. That the DNet model performs worse for large latency spans, where there are more variables, is again probably due to challenges in fitting the DNet model, likely due to some overfitting to the training set.

span.label: only 2 to 8 of 20 hidden units survive regularisation, so the fitted architecture is much smaller than the one specified
span.quote: Although the DNet model had 20 hidden units, the L1 regularization eliminated unnecessary units. Hence there were fewer effective HUs, and for the 25-ms DNet model this number was found to be between 2 and 8

span.label: the data are reused from a previous study rather than collected here
span.quote: The electrophysiological data used in this study were taken from a series of experiments used in a previous study by Harper et al. [ 23 ]. Briefly, recordings were made from the primary auditory cortical areas, A1 and the anterior auditory field (AAF) of 6 adult pigmented ferrets (5 females and 1 male) under ketamine (5 mg/kg/h) and medetomidine (0.022 mg/kg/h) anaesthesia for 20 repeats of the 20 natural sound clips played in random order.

span.label: the firing-rate equation, used to give each network unit a membrane-like time constant
span.quote: Due to the capacitance and resistance of the neural cell membrane, the membrane potential and hence the firing rate is approximately a low-pass filtered version of the synaptic current. A common simple dynamic model of neurons that captures this phenomenon is the differential equation ( Eq 7 ) known as the firing-rate equation

span.label: L1 regularisation, which here does structural work by pruning the network to 2-8 effective units
span.quote: To overcome overfitting, the weights were regularized using an L1-norm (LASSO regularization).

span.label: the cochleagram as a standard front end, so that all compared models see the same transformed input
span.quote: The models receive the input as a cochleagram, a spectrogram-like transformation of the sound waveform. The cochleagram approximates the spectral filtering performed by the auditory periphery

span.label: temporal receptive field here is a MODEL OBJECT - the span of delays a fitted model needs - and the paper's whole argument is that this span need not correspond to delays in the circuit
span.quote: The most direct biological interpretation of the STRF model would involve auditory cortical neurons receiving inputs at a range of simple delays spanning out to 200 ms; however, this is biologically unrealistic.

span.label: time constant in the DNet sits after the nonlinearity and is meant as membrane integration; in the sDNet variant it sits before, and means synaptic integration. Same word, different position, different biology
span.quote: An alternative network model places the integration just before the nonlinearity, which is more consistent with the time constant being synaptic in nature

span.label: effective hidden unit is defined by a variance threshold on its weighted output, so the reported unit counts are post-regularisation and not the specified architecture
span.quote: Although the DNet model had 20 hidden units, the L1 regularization eliminated unnecessary units. Hence there were fewer effective HUs, and for the 25-ms DNet model this number was found to be between 2 and 8

span.label: the 73 analysed neurons are single units surviving a noise-ratio cut of 40, from 549 recorded units of which 284 were single
span.quote: The noise ratio was calculated as a measure of how much the response of each unit is dependent on the stimuli [ 9 , 24 ]. The noise ratio was measured over all 20 stimuli and 20 repeats. Any unit with a noise ratio > 40 were excluded from the study. Also, only putative single units were used. This resulted in 73 neurons for the study.

span.label: cochleagram is a modelled auditory periphery, not a measurement - the input every model sees is already a transformation with chosen parameters
span.quote: The models receive the input as a cochleagram, a spectrogram-like transformation of the sound waveform. The cochleagram approximates the spectral filtering performed by the auditory periphery

span.label: extends → Harper et al. [23] network receptive field (NRF) model
span.quote: This model is the same as a previously published version [ 23 ], except that it uses sigmoid nonlinearities instead of scaled tanh non-linearities.

span.label: replicates → Harper et al. [23] (NRF outperforming the LN model)
span.quote: The NRF model predicts the neural responses equal to or better than the LN model over all durations examined, although by a more modest amount than seen in an earlier study [ 23 ].

span.label: builds-on → the LNFDSNF network model of the salamander retina [45]
span.quote: The LNFDSNF model is particularly relevant to our study because it is a network model whose units have some memory of their past activity, though the form of this memory differs from that of the DNet model.

span.label: critiques → the delay-line reading of spectro-temporal receptive fields extending to 200 ms
span.quote: The most direct biological interpretation of the STRF model would involve auditory cortical neurons receiving inputs at a range of simple delays spanning out to 200 ms; however, this is biologically unrealistic.

span.label: reinterprets → the long inhibitory fields seen in conventional STRFs, as a signature of decaying memory rather than of delayed input
span.quote: When auditory neurons are fitted using a standard LN model, the resulting STRFs often contain narrowband inhibitory fields that decay over approximately 200 ms. In contrast, we find that the STRFs of the DNet model have short inhibitory fields with long time constants. This suggests that these temporally extended inhibitory fields in STRFs may reflect neural mechanisms that can be approximated by exponentially-decaying memory processes.

span.label: extends → earlier work capturing history dependence with synaptic depression
span.quote: There are many biological mechanisms which may underlie exponentially-decaying memory processes. Neurons have various intrinsic dynamic integrative and adaptive characteristics originating from basic membrane dynamics, channel-based adaptation, post-synaptic potentials and short-term synaptic plasticity [ 22 ]. Recurrent network effects could also underlie such memory processes.

span.label: builds-on → Harper et al. 2016, whose ferret recordings are refitted here
span.quote: The electrophysiological data used in this study were taken from a series of experiments used in a previous study by Harper et al. [ 23 ]. Briefly, recordings were made from the primary auditory cortical areas, A1 and the anterior auditory field (AAF) of 6 adult pigmented ferrets (5 females and 1 male) under ketamine (5 mg/kg/h) and medetomidine (0.022 mg/kg/h) anaesthesia for 20 repeats of the 20 natural sound clips played in random order.

span.label: qualifies → its own conclusion, by conceding that long-latency inputs likely contribute as well
span.quote: Hence, we cannot rule out the possibility that long-latency inputs at least partially explain the dependence of auditory cortical neurons on stimulus history–indeed it is likely that they do to some extent.

span.label: STRF —operationalised-as→ delay lines
span.note: the mapping this paper disputes: a fitted delay span is a description, and reading it as circuitry is the step it calls biologically unrealistic
span.quote: The most direct biological interpretation of the STRF model would involve auditory cortical neurons receiving inputs at a range of simple delays spanning out to 200 ms; however, this is biologically unrealistic.

span.label: onset latencies —operationalised-as→ delay lines
span.note: CRITERION: thalamic onset latencies bound what delays can exist - about 14 ms in ferret, 20 in cat, 10 in mouse, 40 in marmoset
span.quote: The onset latencies of neurons in the ventral division of the medial geniculate body (vMGB), which provides the primary ascending input to primary auditory cortex (A1), are typically less than ~14 ms in the ferret [ 18 ], the animal species that provided the data that were modelled in this study. In the cat vMGB response latencies are typically less than ~20 ms [ 19 ], in the mouse less than ~10 ms [ 20 ], and in the marmoset less than ~40 ms

span.label: RETRACTED (DIRECTION REVERSED, and the span states the correct direction explicitly) · DNet —is-a→ NRF model
span.note: RETRACTED: DIRECTION REVERSED, and the span states the correct direction explicitly. `is-a` asserts the subject is subsumed by the object, so `DNet --is-a--> NRF model` claims DNet is a kind of NRF model. The span says the opposite in as many words: 'all possible NRF models are a SUBSET of all possible DNet models' - NRF is inside DNet, DNet is the more general class. The equivalence in the first half of the same span is also SCOPED, not general: the two are equivalent only 'when the discretized time constant for every DNet model unit is at the smallest possible value ( t = 1, d = 0)'. So the edge fails twice over - wrong direction for the subsumption, and unscoped for the equivalence. WHAT THE SPAN DOES SAY (Q-309), now recorded as two edges that split the two claims apart: `NRF model --is-a--> DNet` for the general subsumption, and `DNet --same-as--> NRF model` carrying `holds_when` for the equivalence that holds at one point of the parameter space. Raised by meta-claude as a load-bearing-scope case; reading the span showed the scope was the second fault, not the first. — the NRF is the DNet with every time constant at minimum, which is why the DNet losing to it is a fitting artefact and not a finding
span.quote: Note that the DNet model is equivalent to the NRF model when the discretized time constant for every DNet model unit is at the smallest possible value ( τ = 1, d = 0). Hence, because all possible NRF models are a subset of all possible DNet models, the DNet should in theory always equal or outperform the NRF model.

span.label: time constant —operationalised-as→ membrane time constant
span.note: intended as membrane integration but explicitly not exclusive of channel adaptation, synaptic depression or recurrence
span.quote: We note, however, that although the DNet model was developed with membrane dynamics in mind, aspects of all the above listed dynamic processes could be captured by the same exponentially-decaying memory in the DNet. These different processes are not exclusive of each other, and combinations of them may contribute to the effects we find.

span.label: DNet —contrasted-with→ sDNet
span.note: CRITERION: decay after the nonlinearity beats decay before it, which is the membrane versus synaptic distinction made testable
span.quote: The sDNet model achieves best performance in predicting neural responses when the duration of the STRFs is 200 ms (CC norm = 0.71) ( Fig 8A ). Although the sDNet with 25-ms STRFs predicts neural responses better (CC norm = 0.67) than the 25-ms LN model (CC norm = 0.51) and the 25-ms NRF model (CC norm = 0.51), it is worse than the 25-ms DNet model (CC norm = 0.71). This suggests that a large percentage of the variance of neural responses can be explained by a time constant before non-linearity, but that having a time constant after the non-linearity further improves prediction.

span.label: time constant —causes→ IE score
span.note: not built in: the units that end up with long memories are almost all inhibitory
span.quote: We found that almost all units having large time constants are inhibitory in nature

span.label: LASSO regularization —causes→ hidden units
span.note: SIGN: prunes. 20 specified units become 2-8 effective ones, so the fitted model is not the stated architecture
span.quote: Although the DNet model had 20 hidden units, the L1 regularization eliminated unnecessary units. Hence there were fewer effective HUs, and for the 25-ms DNet model this number was found to be between 2 and 8

span.label: noise ratio —operationalised-as→ A1
span.note: the inclusion rule that turns 549 recorded units into the 73 the paper is about
span.quote: The noise ratio was calculated as a measure of how much the response of each unit is dependent on the stimuli [ 9 , 24 ]. The noise ratio was measured over all 20 stimuli and 20 repeats. Any unit with a noise ratio > 40 were excluded from the study. Also, only putative single units were used. This resulted in 73 neurons for the study.

span.label: cochleagram —part-of→ STRF
span.note: every model shares this front end, so all comparisons are conditional on the same modelled periphery
span.quote: The models receive the input as a cochleagram, a spectrogram-like transformation of the sound waveform. The cochleagram approximates the spectral filtering performed by the auditory periphery

span.label: stimulus history —operationalised-as→ time constant
span.note: the paper's central substitution: history dependence rendered as decaying memory rather than as stored delays
span.quote: These findings suggest that integration due to the membrane time constants or other exponentially-decaying memory processes may underlie linear temporal receptive fields of neurons beyond 25 ms.

span.label: short term synaptic plasticity —same-as→ time constant
span.note: one of several processes the same fitted decay could be; weight low because the paper declines to distinguish them
span.quote: We note, however, that although the DNet model was developed with membrane dynamics in mind, aspects of all the above listed dynamic processes could be captured by the same exponentially-decaying memory in the DNet. These different processes are not exclusive of each other, and combinations of them may contribute to the effects we find.

span.label: NRF model —is-a→ DNet
span.quote: because all possible NRF models are a subset of all possible DNet models, the DNet should in theory always equal or outperform the NRF model.

span.label: DNet —same-as→ NRF model
span.quote: Note that the DNet model is equivalent to the NRF model when the discretized time constant for every DNet model unit is at the smallest possible value ( τ = 1, d = 0).

span.label: correlation coefficient
span.quote: For each of the fitted models, neural responses were then predicted for the validation set, and the correlation coefficient between the actual neural responses and the prediction was measured.

span.label: Pearson correlation
span.quote: The means of non-normalized Pearson correlation coefficients (CC) are 0.40, 0.50, 0.54, 0.55, and 0.55 respectively.

span.label: k-fold cross-validation
span.quote: The cross-validation set (the remaining 16 stimuli) was used to fit the models using k -fold cross validation, where k = 8.

span.label: standard error of the mean
span.quote: Each black dot represents a neuron, the curve indicates the mean over 73 neurons and error bars indicate standard error of the mean.

span.label: regularized regression (LASSO / L1)
span.quote: To overcome overfitting, the weights were regularized using an L1-norm (LASSO regularization).

span.label: linear regression
span.quote: Both w and b are free parameters of the model and were estimated by regressing neural response y(t) against input x ( t ) using glmnet

span.label: held-out test set
span.quote: From the data for the 20 sound stimuli, 4 were chosen as a test set which was not used during training and cross-validation.

span.label: LASSO regularization
span.quote: To overcome overfitting, the weights were regularized using an L1-norm (LASSO regularization).

span.label: cross-validation
span.quote: To overcome overfitting, the weights were regularized using an L1-norm (LASSO regularization).

span.label: CC norm
span.quote: The 25-ms DNet model out performs the DNet with longer (200 ms and 400 ms) STRFs, as measured by prediction of neural responses on a held-out test set averaged over all 73 neurons ( Fig 5A ). It also achieves performance similar to the best performing LN model, but performs a little worse than the best performing NRF model

span.label: A linear-nonlinear STRF model needs delay lines reaching at least 200 ms into the past to predict A1 responses well, a span the authors argue is biologically unrealistic.
span.quote: For a linear-non-linear STRF model (LN model) to achieve a high level of performance in predicting single unit neural responses to natural sounds in the primary auditory cortex, we found that it is necessary to include time delays going back at least 200 ms in the past.

span.label: A dynamic network whose units carry exponentially decaying memory reaches the same held-out prediction performance with only 25 ms of STRF as the best 200 ms LN model.
span.quote: We find that this dynamic network (DNet) model, when fitted to the neural data using STRFs of only 25 ms duration, can achieve prediction performance on a held-out dataset comparable to the best performing LN model with STRFs of 200 ms duration.

span.label: Lengthening the DNet's STRFs does not help and slightly hurts: the 25 ms version beats the 200 ms and 400 ms versions on held-out data.
span.quote: The 25-ms DNet model out performs the DNet with longer (200 ms and 400 ms) STRFs, as measured by prediction of neural responses on a held-out test set averaged over all 73 neurons

span.label: Silencing the hidden units whose time constants exceed the STRF duration damages the 25 ms DNet more than any other version, showing that the long time constants are what carry its stimulus-history dependence.
span.quote: We found that the 25-ms DNet model is the DNet whose CC norm is most reduced by this alteration

span.label: A single dynamic unit with one STRF predicts worse than the LN model, so long time constants only work when embedded in a multi-unit network.
span.quote: This indicates that both long time constants and a network architecture are needed for the 25-ms DNet model to achieve prediction performance similar to that of standard models.

span.label: Hidden units carrying long time constants are almost all inhibitory in their effect on the output unit.
span.quote: We found that almost all units having large time constants are inhibitory in nature

span.label: Placing the exponential integration before the nonlinearity (the synaptic-style sDNet) is better than static 25 ms models but worse than integrating after the nonlinearity as the DNet does.
span.quote: Although the sDNet with 25-ms STRFs predicts neural responses better (CC norm = 0.67) than the 25-ms LN model (CC norm = 0.51) and the 25-ms NRF model (CC norm = 0.51), it is worse than the 25-ms DNet model (CC norm = 0.71).

span.label: L1 regularization left only between 2 and 8 hidden units effective per neuron in the 25 ms DNet, so the succinct fit uses very few components.
span.quote: Hence there were fewer effective HUs, and for the 25-ms DNet model this number was found to be between 2 and 8

span.label: The fitted time constants of effective hidden units spanned 5 to 475 ms, far exceeding the 25 ms STRF window they accompany.
span.quote: In the 25-ms DNet model, the time constants of the effective HUs ranged between 5 and 475 ms, often far greater than the duration of the STRFs

span.label: a 25 ms DNet matched the best 200 ms LN model on held-out prediction
span.quote: We find that this dynamic network (DNet) model, when fitted to the neural data using STRFs of only 25 ms duration, can achieve prediction performance on a held-out dataset comparable to the best performing LN model with STRFs of 200 ms duration.

span.label: the 25 ms DNet beat 25 ms LN and NRF models by a large margin, and beat DNets with longer delay spans
span.quote: Also, the 25-ms LN and NRF models are outperformed by a large margin by the 25-ms DNet model ( Fig 5A ). A neuron by neuron comparison shows that this result is also consistent for almost all neurons

span.label: it performed slightly worse than the best NRF model, which the paper attributes to fitting rather than to the model class
span.quote: The 25-ms DNet model out performs the DNet with longer (200 ms and 400 ms) STRFs, as measured by prediction of neural responses on a held-out test set averaged over all 73 neurons ( Fig 5A ). It also achieves performance similar to the best performing LN model, but performs a little worse than the best performing NRF model

span.label: NESTED-MODEL VIOLATION DIAGNOSED: the DNet contains the NRF as a special case, so losing to it must be an optimisation failure
span.quote: The fact that this is not the case suggests that, at least in some cases, the very best fits are not being found for the DNet model, perhaps as a consequence of some overfitting. That the DNet model performs worse for large latency spans, where there are more variables, is again probably due to challenges in fitting the DNet model, likely due to some overfitting to the training set.

span.label: removing units whose time constants exceed their delay span hurt the 25 ms DNet most, showing the long memories carry the work
span.quote: To understand how much of an effect HUs of the DNet model with long time constants have on the model’s predictions, the fitted model was modified by ‘knocking out’ (see Methods ) HUs with time constants longer than the duration of their STRFs. This was achieved by setting the output weights of those units to zero, while keeping all other parameters intact. We found that the 25-ms DNet model is the DNet whose CC norm is most reduced by this alteration

span.label: a single dynamic unit performed worse than a plain LN model, so decay alone is not enough without a network
span.quote: A single-unit dynamic model was also developed to examine the effect of a time constant in an LN-like single STRF model. Prediction performance of this model was found to be worse than the LN model ( Fig 6B ). This indicates that both long time constants and a network architecture are needed for the 25-ms DNet model to achieve prediction performance similar to that of standard models.

span.label: fitted time constants ran from 5 to 475 ms, far exceeding the 25 ms delay span
span.quote: In the 25-ms DNet model, the time constants of the effective HUs ranged between 5 and 475 ms, often far greater than the duration of the STRFs

span.label: almost all units with long time constants turned out inhibitory
span.quote: We found that almost all units having large time constants are inhibitory in nature

span.label: more effective hidden units tended to have longer time constants
span.quote: This showed that high-ranked HUs tend to have long time constants

span.label: putting the decay before the nonlinearity was worse than after, favouring a membrane over a synaptic reading
span.quote: The sDNet model achieves best performance in predicting neural responses when the duration of the STRFs is 200 ms (CC norm = 0.71) ( Fig 8A ). Although the sDNet with 25-ms STRFs predicts neural responses better (CC norm = 0.67) than the 25-ms LN model (CC norm = 0.51) and the 25-ms NRF model (CC norm = 0.51), it is worse than the 25-ms DNet model (CC norm = 0.71). This suggests that a large percentage of the variance of neural responses can be explained by a time constant before non-linearity, but that having a time constant after the non-linearity further improves prediction.

span.label: REINTERPRETATION: the long inhibitory fields in conventional STRFs may be decaying memory rather than delayed inhibition
span.quote: When auditory neurons are fitted using a standard LN model, the resulting STRFs often contain narrowband inhibitory fields that decay over approximately 200 ms. In contrast, we find that the STRFs of the DNet model have short inhibitory fields with long time constants. This suggests that these temporally extended inhibitory fields in STRFs may reflect neural mechanisms that can be approximated by exponentially-decaying memory processes.

span.label: CONCEDED: long-latency thalamic inputs cannot be excluded and probably contribute
span.quote: Hence, we cannot rule out the possibility that long-latency inputs at least partially explain the dependence of auditory cortical neurons on stimulus history–indeed it is likely that they do to some extent.

span.label: STATED SCOPE LIMIT: dependence out to about 4 seconds is beyond this model because its memory is exponential
span.quote: The firing rate of A1 neurons has been demonstrated to depend on stimulus history up to ~4 s in the past [ 17 ]. This dependence cannot be fully captured by linear models such as STRFs (17). This indicates that there are some nonlinear dynamic processes that provide history dependence which cannot be captured either by a linear or LN models, nor by the DNet model. Perhaps this is because the DNet model has limited capacity to capture temporal dynamics that are not exponential in nature.

span.label: spectro-temporal receptive field (STRF) model
span.quote: The tuning properties of auditory neurons are commonly described by a spectro-temporal receptive field (STRF) model, which characterizes the linear dependence of the neural response on the sound spectrum at a range of latencies

span.label: dynamic network (DNet) model
span.quote: We constructed a neural-network model whose output is the weighted sum of units whose responses are determined by a dynamic firing-rate equation.

span.label: network receptive field (NRF) model
span.quote: The NRF model is an artificial neural network with a single hidden layer of 20 hidden units (HU) which converge onto an output unit (OU).

span.label: sDNet (synaptic dynamic network) model
span.quote: Hence, in the sDNet model, the activation of each HU, rather than the output of the nonlinearity, is convolved with an exponential decay impulse response.

span.label: cochleagram
span.quote: The models receive the input as a cochleagram, a spectrogram-like transformation of the sound waveform.

span.label: noise ratio
span.quote: The noise ratio was calculated as a measure of how much the response of each unit is dependent on the stimuli

span.label: effective hidden unit
span.quote: Any HU with variance greater than 5% of the sum of the variances of all 20 HUs is considered effective.

span.label: firing-rate equation
span.quote: A common simple dynamic model of neurons that captures this phenomenon is the differential equation ( Eq 7 ) known as the firing-rate equation [ 22 ].

span.label: LN model
span.quote: The two stage LN model consists of a linear model followed by a sigmoid output nonlinearity.

span.label: NRF model
span.quote: The NRF model is an artificial neural network with a single hidden layer of 20 hidden units (HU) which converge onto an output unit (OU). Each unit of the model is similar to a single LN model.

span.label: cochleagram
span.quote: The models receive the input as a cochleagram, a spectrogram-like transformation of the sound waveform. The cochleagram approximates the spectral filtering performed by the auditory periphery

span.label: noise ratio
span.quote: The noise ratio was calculated as a measure of how much the response of each unit is dependent on the stimuli [ 9 , 24 ]. The noise ratio was measured over all 20 stimuli and 20 repeats. Any unit with a noise ratio > 40 were excluded from the study. Also, only putative single units were used. This resulted in 73 neurons for the study.

span.label: time constant
span.quote: Due to the capacitance and resistance of the neural cell membrane, the membrane potential and hence the firing rate is approximately a low-pass filtered version of the synaptic current. A common simple dynamic model of neurons that captures this phenomenon is the differential equation ( Eq 7 ) known as the firing-rate equation

span.label: span of latencies (duration) of the model STRF
span.term: span of latencies (duration) of the model STRF
span.quote: The effect of different spans of latencies (lengths) of the STRF was investigated.

span.label: knocking out hidden units whose time constants exceed the STRF duration
span.term: knocking out hidden units whose time constants exceed the STRF duration
span.quote: This was achieved by setting the output weights of those units to zero, while keeping all other parameters intact.

span.label: prediction performance on held-out neural responses (CC norm)
span.term: prediction performance on held-out neural responses (CC norm)
span.quote: For each of the fitted models, neural responses were then predicted for the validation set, and the correlation coefficient between the actual neural responses and the prediction was measured.

span.label: amount of training data (duration of neural response) given to each model
span.term: amount of training data (duration of neural response) given to each model
span.quote: To ensure that all models receive the same amount of training data, models with different latency spans of STRFs are provided with exactly the same durations of neural response.

span.label: time constant
span.quote: In the 25-ms DNet model, the time constants of the effective HUs ranged between 5 and 475 ms, often far greater than the duration of the STRFs

span.label: STRF
span.quote: We find that this dynamic network (DNet) model, when fitted to the neural data using STRFs of only 25 ms duration, can achieve prediction performance on a held-out dataset comparable to the best performing LN model with STRFs of 200 ms duration.

span.label: IE score
span.quote: We found that almost all units having large time constants are inhibitory in nature

span.label: 0.51, 0.64, 0.69, 0.71, and 0.71 — mean normalized correlation coefficient of the LN model on held-out data for STRF lengths of 25, 50, 100, 200 and 400 ms — performance saturates only at 200 ms
span.quote: the mean normalized correlation coefficient, mean CC norm [ 30 , 31 ], between the actual neural responses and the prediction of LN models with 25, 50, 100, 200, and 400 ms long STRFs are respectively 0.51, 0.64, 0.69, 0.71, and 0.71

span.label: 0.71, 0.71, 0.70, 0.68 and 0.68 — mean normalized correlation coefficient of the DNet model for the same STRF lengths — already maximal at 25 ms
span.quote: We found that the mean CC norm between the actual neural responses and the predictions of the DNet model with 25, 50, 100, 200 and 400 ms STRFs are respectively 0.71, 0.71, 0.70, 0.68 and 0.68

span.label: 0.40, 0.50, 0.54, 0.55, and 0.55 — mean raw (non-normalized) Pearson correlation coefficients for the LN model across the five STRF lengths
span.quote: The means of non-normalized Pearson correlation coefficients (CC) are 0.40, 0.50, 0.54, 0.55, and 0.55 respectively.

span.label: 73 — single units that passed the noise-ratio criterion and were modelled
span.quote: This resulted in 73 neurons for the study.

span.label: 549 / 284 — single and multi-units recorded in 56 penetrations, of which 284 were single units
span.quote: In total, 56 penetrations resulted in 549 single and multi-units, of which 284 were single units.

span.label: CC norm = 0.71 — best sDNet performance, reached only with 200 ms STRFs, versus the DNet reaching the same value at 25 ms
span.quote: The sDNet model achieves best performance in predicting neural responses when the duration of the STRFs is 200 ms (CC norm = 0.71)

span.label: ~30% — share of the normalized correlation coefficient still unexplained by the DNet model
span.quote: provides a basis from which to develop further models to account for the ~30% of the CC norm that remains to be explained

span.label: 25 ms against 200 ms — delay span the DNet needs against the span the LN model needs for the same prediction
span.quote: We find that this dynamic network (DNet) model, when fitted to the neural data using STRFs of only 25 ms duration, can achieve prediction performance on a held-out dataset comparable to the best performing LN model with STRFs of 200 ms duration.

span.label: ~14 ms — typical thalamic onset latency in ferret, the species modelled - the bound that makes 200 ms delays implausible
span.quote: The onset latencies of neurons in the ventral division of the medial geniculate body (vMGB), which provides the primary ascending input to primary auditory cortex (A1), are typically less than ~14 ms in the ferret [ 18 ], the animal species that provided the data that were modelled in this study. In the cat vMGB response latencies are typically less than ~20 ms [ 19 ], in the mouse less than ~10 ms [ 20 ], and in the marmoset less than ~40 ms

span.label: 5 to 475 ms — range of fitted time constants among effective hidden units
span.quote: In the 25-ms DNet model, the time constants of the effective HUs ranged between 5 and 475 ms, often far greater than the duration of the STRFs

span.label: 2 to 8 of 20 — hidden units surviving regularisation per neuron
span.quote: Although the DNet model had 20 hidden units, the L1 regularization eliminated unnecessary units. Hence there were fewer effective HUs, and for the 25-ms DNet model this number was found to be between 2 and 8

span.label: 73 of 549 — units analysed after the single-unit and noise-ratio criteria
span.quote: The noise ratio was calculated as a measure of how much the response of each unit is dependent on the stimuli [ 9 , 24 ]. The noise ratio was measured over all 20 stimuli and 20 repeats. Any unit with a noise ratio > 40 were excluded from the study. Also, only putative single units were used. This resulted in 73 neurons for the study.

span.label: ~4 s — how far back A1 responses are known to depend on history, beyond this model's reach
span.quote: The firing rate of A1 neurons has been demonstrated to depend on stimulus history up to ~4 s in the past [ 17 ]. This dependence cannot be fully captured by linear models such as STRFs (17). This indicates that there are some nonlinear dynamic processes that provide history dependence which cannot be captured either by a linear or LN models, nor by the DNet model. Perhaps this is because the DNet model has limited capacity to capture temporal dynamics that are not exponential in nature.
